summary: Describes how URI signing can enforce content access control between interconnected content delivery networks (CDNI). It proposes a method built as a profile of JSON Web Tokens (JWT), specifying where the signed token travels in the URI and which claims it must hold so a user agent can be authorized to fetch content. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A concert ticket has a stamp only the venue can make. A signed web link works the same way: it carries a stamp that proves you are allowed in, so the helper servers can check it.

questions: how does cdni uri signing work
how to sign urls with jwt for cdn access control
how does uri signing work in cdn
subtitle: How a signed token inside a URL lets a content provider and a chain of CDNs agree on who may fetch what.

tldr.problem: When a content provider hands delivery to a CDN, and that CDN hands it on to another CDN, every network in the chain needs a way to check that each individual request was authorized by the provider.
tldr.mechanism: The URI carries a signed JSON Web Token (JWT) whose claims, such as expiry time, client IP address and a URI pattern, are checked by each CDN. The upstream CDN re-signs the URI when it redirects the client to a downstream CDN.
tldr.outcome: CDNs can enforce a provider's per-request policy without knowing the policy itself. The scheme is not content protection, and shared secret keys are NOT RECOMMENDED.

today: RFC 9246 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2022, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why URIs Get Signed
sections.content:
RFC 9246 describes URI Signing: a way to make sure only authorized user agents (UAs) can fetch content when a Content Service Provider (CSP) redirects them to a CDN, or when one CDN redirects them to another. The CSP can authorize every individual request.

The RFC is explicit that URI Signing is not a content protection scheme. If a CSP wants to protect the content itself, mechanisms such as Digital Rights Management (DRM) are more appropriate. A side benefit is a smaller impact from denial-of-service attacks.

The method is built on signed JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) from RFC 7519. It splits two roles: the CSP initiates per-request authorization, and the CDN verifies it. That lets any distribution policy be enforced across CDNs without the CDNs knowing the CSP's specific policies.
sections.plainLanguage: A website wants to give out tickets to its videos, and the helper servers that actually hand over the videos need to check the tickets. This document says how to make a ticket that every helper can check.

sections.title: Trust, Keys and CDN Interconnection
sections.content:
In the simple case the CSP redirects the UA to a CDN with a Target CDN URI that holds a signed JWT. The CDN verifies the JWT, checks any time window and URI pattern, then delivers the content. In the CDNI case there is an upstream CDN (uCDN) and a downstream CDN (dCDN). The uCDN can sign a Redirection URI that sends the UA on to the dCDN.

Two kinds of keys can sign the JWT. With an asymmetric key pair, only the signer holds the private key, and the public key can be handed out openly. With a symmetric shared key, signer and verifier use the same secret, which must be kept confidential. Shared keys MUST NOT be redistributed, and using one is supported but NOT RECOMMENDED.

The kind of request routing matters. With DNS-based routing the CSP's Signed URI reaches the dCDN directly, so a dCDN with no relationship to the CSP needs asymmetric keys. With HTTP-based routing the uCDN verifies the URI and signs a new one, so either key type works because the uCDN and dCDN always have a relationship. A signed Redirection URI MUST keep HTTPS as the scheme if the original had it.

The method was created for CDNI but nothing stops it being used with a single CDN, for example to let a CSP that uses several CDNs implement one signing mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to make a stamp. One uses a secret stamp that only you hold, with a picture anyone can check. The other shares one secret stamp with everyone, which is risky because one leak ruins it.

sections.title: The Token and Its Claims
sections.content:
The signed JWT travels in a URI attribute called the URI Signing Package, as either a path-style or a form-style parameter. Both styles MUST be supported. The parameter name comes from CDNI Metadata or from configuration, for example token in http://example.com/media/path?come=data&token=SIGNEDJWT&other=data. Clocks of the signer and verifier MUST be in sync, and the RFC recommends NTP.

All claims below are mandatory to implement, but only cdniuc MUST be present in every token. Standard claims follow RFC 7519:

  • iss, aud, jti: issuer, intended recipient and a unique ID. A jti can stop replay if the CDN remembers used values.
  • exp and nbf: the request is rejected outside the window, and no time-synchronization leeway is allowed.
  • sub: if used, MUST be an encrypted JWE object because it holds personally identifiable information.

New CDNI claims:

  • cdniv: claim set version, which MUST be 1 for this specification.
  • cdnicrit: lists extension claims the recipient MUST understand, or reject the token.
  • cdniip: the client IP address or prefix, also an encrypted JWE. Use at large is NOT RECOMMENDED, because addresses change with dual-stack, MPTCP, QUIC and Wi-Fi to cellular switches.
  • cdniuc: the URI container, either hash: (a URL-segment hash of the URI) or regex: (a POSIX extended regular expression). Before matching, the signed JWT is removed from the URI and the URI is normalized.
  • cdniets, cdnistt, cdnistd: settings for token renewal, described later.

When a CDN generates a new JWT for redirection, many claims have carry-over rules. For example, a sub, exp, nbf or cdniip claim MUST be copied unchanged if present and MUST NOT be added if absent.
sections.plainLanguage: The ticket lists rules, like "good only until 5 o'clock" or "only for this one door". The helper checks every rule and says no if any one fails.

sections.title: Token Renewal for Segmented Video
sections.content:
Streaming protocols such as MPEG-DASH and HTTP Live Streaming split a video into small segments listed in a manifest. Requests for segments come from the manifest and are not redirected, so a malicious UA could share the manifest and deep-link to segments. Putting a Signed URI for every segment in the manifest would force the CDN to rewrite it for each UA, and the URIs would need a long validity, for example at least 30 minutes for a long stream.

Signed Token Renewal avoids this. When a UA successfully fetches a segment, the HTTP 2xx response carries a fresh signed JWT to use for the next one. Because the next segment cannot be predicted (seeking, switching representation), the regex: container lets one token cover many URLs.

Three claims control it. cdniets is the number of seconds added to the verification time to give the next token's exp. cdnistt says how the token is transported: 0 is not enabled, 1 is a cookie and 2 is the query string. cdnistd is the number of path segments that must match, with zero meaning any path. Both cdnistt and cdniets MUST be present for renewal.

With value 1 the token is sent in a URISigningPackage cookie on the 2xx or 3xx response, which lets legacy UAs take part. Cross-domain cookies are not supported in some environments, so for a redirect to another domain the query string SHOULD be used and cdnistt MUST be 2. Any redirection between domains has to happen while fetching the manifest.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a ride with many gates. Each time you pass a gate, the attendant hands you a fresh short-lived ticket for the next one, so nobody can copy one ticket and use it all day.

sections.title: How It Plugs Into the CDNI Interfaces
sections.content:
A dCDN that supports URI Signing must be able to advertise that to the uCDN, and the uCDN must be able to pass the information needed to verify Signed URIs. The Control interface and the Request Routing Redirection interface (RFC 7975) are not affected. Capability advertisement reuses the Footprint and Capabilities interface of RFC 8008.

The Metadata interface (RFC 8006) gets a new MI.UriSigning object with four properties:

  • enforce: a boolean, default true. When false, the dCDN does no verification.
  • issuers: valid issuers, default an empty list, which accepts any issuer in the trusted key store.
  • package-attribute: the parameter name, default URISigningPackage.
  • jwt-header: a JWT header supplied out of band, which shortens the token.

The Logging interface (RFC 7937) gets a new record type, cdni_http_request_v2, with two fields: s-uri-signing, a 3-digit verification code, and an optional s-uri-signing-deny-reason string.
sections.plainLanguage: The helpers need a way to tell each other they know how to check tickets, to share the rules for checking them, and to write down who got turned away and why.

sections.title: The Message Flow
sections.content:
With HTTP-based routing and two CDNs, the steps are: the dCDN advertises URI Signing support (step 1), the CSP gives the uCDN verification keys (2), and the uCDN passes verification information to the dCDN through Metadata (3). Later, the UA asks the CSP for content and the CSP decides. A negative decision gets an error such as 403 Forbidden. A positive one returns a Signed URI.

The UA sends that URI to the uCDN, which verifies it and answers 403 Forbidden on failure. On success the uCDN signs a new URI and redirects the UA to the dCDN, which verifies it again before delivering. Later the dCDN reports log events.

With DNS-based routing, the UA gets the Signed URI from the CSP, asks the uCDN's DNS, is redirected to the dCDN's DNS, gets a Surrogate address and sends the content request there. The dCDN verifies the JWT itself. This works with asymmetric keys. With symmetric keys the key would have to travel to CDNs the CSP may not trust, and the RFC says this architecture MUST NOT be implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask the owner for a ticket, show it at the first desk, get a new ticket pointing to the second desk, and show that one to get your item. Each desk checks its own ticket.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the MI.UriSigning CDNI Payload Type and the cdni_http_request_v2 logging record type. It added the two new logging field names and created two subregistries under the CDNI Parameters registry, both with a Specification Required policy.

The URI Signing Verification Code subregistry gives the meaning of s-uri-signing. The other subregistry, Signed Token Transport, defines the cdnistt values 0, 1 and 2. The RFC also registers the claims cdniv, cdnicrit, cdniip, cdniuc, cdniets, cdnistt and cdnistd in the JSON Web Token Claims registry, with guidance that Expert Reviewers should allow new claims that do not conflict with existing ones.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are written in a public list so everyone uses the same numbers for the same meanings.

sections.title: Limits, Attacks and Privacy
sections.content:
Including more claims raises protection, but URI Signing has known limits. JWT guidance in RFC 8725 applies.

  • Replay: a valid Signed URI can be replayed. A short gap between nbf and exp helps, though a couple of seconds are needed for network hiccups. A one-time jti lets the dCDN reject reuse, as long as the used-ID list is kept bounded.
  • NAT: users behind one NAT share an IP address, so cdniip cannot tell them apart.
  • Shared keys: a shared key is more likely to be compromised and is highly discouraged in new implementations. A stolen signing key can also be used to force the CDN to evaluate expensive regular expressions in cdniuc, so compromised keys should be revoked promptly. Regex evaluation is best done after the JWT is verified.
  • Wildcard container: since cdniuc is the only mandatory claim, a wildcard value makes a skeleton key. This is NOT RECOMMENDED, and only revoking the signing key stops it.

On privacy, the client IP and subject are encrypted before being put in the URI.
sections.plainLanguage: A ticket can still be copied or lent, and a leaked stamp can print tickets for anything. So keep tickets short-lived and keep the stamp secret.
